title: General Dentist vs Endodontist: Who Should Do Your Root Canal?
metaTitle: General Dentist vs Endodontist for a Root Canal
metaDescription: Can a general dentist do your root canal, or do you need an endodontist? Learn how dentists decide, when cases are referred, and what it means for you.
primaryKeyword: general dentist vs endodontist root canal
secondaryKeywords: can a general dentist do a root canal
excerpt: How to tell whether a general dentist or an endodontist should perform your root canal, and how that decision is made.
heroImageAlt: A dentist examining a molar model while explaining root canal options to a patient.
bodyHtml:
A general dentist can perform your root canal in many cases, and you do not automatically need an endodontist. Most straightforward root canals are carried out by general dentists, while an endodontist — a dentist with additional specialty training focused on the inside of the tooth — tends to handle more complex or difficult cases, retreatments, and some surgical procedures. Which professional is right for you depends on the tooth, its anatomy, and your individual situation, and your dentist will help you decide.

What a general dentist does

General and family dentists are trained to diagnose and treat a broad range of dental problems, including root canal therapy on many teeth. For a tooth with relatively simple canal anatomy and a clear diagnosis, a general dentist is often well suited to carry out the treatment from start to finish, including planning the crown or filling that protects the tooth afterward.

What an endodontist adds

An endodontist is a dental specialist who has completed additional years of training concentrated on the pulp and the tissues around the root. Endodontists often use specialised tools and spend their days focused on these procedures, which makes them a sensible choice for teeth with unusual or curved canals, calcified canals, previous root canals that need redoing, or cases requiring surgery such as an apicoectomy.

How the decision is usually made

Your dentist weighs several factors when deciding whether to treat a tooth or refer it:

  • Tooth type and anatomy. Front teeth usually have a single canal, while molars have more and can be more intricate.
  • Complexity. Narrow, curved, or calcified canals can be harder to navigate.
  • History. A tooth that has had a root canal before and is causing trouble again may benefit from specialist retreatment.
  • Your health and comfort. Medical factors and anxiety levels can influence the plan.

Being referred is a normal, responsible part of dental care. It reflects a dentist matching the treatment to the tooth rather than any shortcoming.

What this means for your appointment

In practice, you do not have to sort any of this out yourself. At a consultation, the dentist examines the tooth, reviews the X-rays, and tells you whether they are comfortable treating it or would prefer to involve a specialist. It is completely reasonable to ask directly, "Will you be doing this, or referring me, and why?" A clear answer helps you understand the plan and opens the door to other useful questions about timing, the number of visits, and how the tooth will be rebuilt afterward. You can also ask what would change if the tooth turned out to be more complex than it first appears, so there are no surprises midway through the process.

Does the outcome depend on who does it?

Research and professional bodies such as the American Association of Endodontists emphasise that good outcomes depend on accurate diagnosis, thorough cleaning and sealing of the canals, and a well-fitted final restoration. Both general dentists and endodontists aim for these standards. The key is that the person treating your tooth is comfortable with its complexity.

Where Dr. Kadivar fits in

At Smile Dental Arts Centre in Markham, Dr. Neda Kadivar is a general and family dentist with over 20 years of experience who provides root canal treatment at the clinic. For cases that call for specialist involvement, more complex teeth may be referred to an endodontist, which is standard practice across general dentistry. You can read more about the clinic's approach to root canals and related care on its endodontics services page.

Can a general dentist do a molar root canal?

Yes, many do. Molars are more complex than front teeth, so the dentist will assess the canal anatomy and decide whether to treat the tooth or refer it to a specialist.

Is an endodontist always better?

Not necessarily. For straightforward teeth, a general dentist is often entirely appropriate. Specialists add value mainly for difficult, repeat, or surgical cases.

Will a referral cost me more time?

It can add an appointment, but it may also improve the chance of a smooth result for a complicated tooth. Ask your dentist to explain the reasoning.

If you are unsure which route suits your tooth, a consultation is the best starting point. The team at Smile Dental Arts Centre can examine the tooth, review X-rays, and recommend whether treatment in the clinic or a referral makes the most sense for you.

This article is general information and not a substitute for professional dental advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always speak with a licensed dentist about your specific situation.
